Interval Arithmetic Inclusion Strategies compute conservative bounds on an implicit function $f$ over a spatial domain, enabling the bisection trace to prune intervals that cannot contain the zero-level set [S1, unofficial].

The evidence explicitly states that 'isoray' uses 'interval-arithmetic bisection' to render the 'zero-level-set' of an implicit function. It lists four 'inclusion strategies' (SamplingInclusion, GradientInclusion, NaturalIntervalInclusion, AffineInclusion) that compute 'interval bounds' (conservative bounds) of the function. The text confirms that these strategies provide 'tighter bounds' (optimization) and that the method ensures 'no surface features are missed' (robustness), which implies the pruning of intervals that do not contain the solution (zero-level set). The claim accurately reflects the functionality described in the source.

These strategies were developed to guarantee no surface features are missed (e.g., thin shells, cusps, high-frequency surfaces) while optimizing performance through tighter bounds when analytic formulas are known [S1, unofficial].

It also states that 'When the analytic formula is known, Natural Interval Arithmetic (NIA) and Affine Arithmetic (AA) provide tighter bounds as an optimization path' (supporting the second part of the claim regarding optimizing performance through tighter bounds when analytic formulas are known).

They distinguish themselves from sibling methods by providing a configurable trade-off between generality (black-box compatibility) and bound tightness (performance/accuracy), spanning sampling-based estimates to analytic arithmetic [S1, unofficial].

This directly supports the claim of a configurable trade-off spanning sampling-based estimates to analytic arithmetic.
